venue: Delta Center, Salt Lake City, UT, United States

items.fight_news: Silva's championship path depends on whether she can keep Wang turning rather than planted. Her lateral exits, calf-kick timing, and stance-switching looks can make Wang reset, but every exit has to be disciplined because Wang's counter windows are most dangerous when opponents admire their work.

Wang needs to make the fight less about chasing and more about trapping. If she can cut the cage, jab to the body, and make Silva exchange after the second layer, the title fight shifts from movement control into a power-and-durability test.

Five rounds create the biggest model question for Silva. Her best three-round version can win on activity and distance management, but championship minutes ask whether she can keep enough pop on counters to stop Wang from walking through late entries.

The live tell is Wang's reaction to Silva's first clean angle change. If Wang pivots with her and keeps her lead hand active, she can pressure without overreaching; if she follows in straight lines, Silva's kick-and-exit game can build a lead fast.

Figueiredo's best premium lane is making Talbott respect layered threats early: calf kicks, sudden level changes, and clinch breaks that interrupt Talbott's preferred rhythm. If Talbott gets to build volume without defensive resets, the younger fighter's pace becomes harder to slow.

Talbott should target efficiency over spectacle. Figueiredo is still dangerous in compressed exchanges, so Talbott's cleanest path is long combinations, immediate exits, and forcing the former champion to restart rather than giving him pocket moments to explode through.

The grappling threat may matter even if neither fighter spends long stretches on the mat. Figueiredo can use takedown looks to make Talbott hesitate, while Talbott can answer by winning underhook battles and turning breaks into volume.

Green's defensive style rewards him when opponents attack one beat at a time. Ribovics has to combine body work, low kicks, and layered entries so Green cannot simply read the shoulders and counter from his preferred pocket rhythm.

Ribovics' aggression is valuable only if it stays organized. If he overextends after early success, Green can turn the fight into a timing lesson with pull counters, short exits, and scoreable jabs that make pressure look inefficient.

The judging hinge is optics versus impact. Green often wins clean-looking exchanges even at lower damage, while Ribovics can sway rounds with visible force if he lands to the body and legs before hunting the head.

Williams' right hand is most dangerous when opponents retreat in straight lines, so Soldic's footwork after his own left hand is the first premium read. If Soldic exits square, Williams can close fast; if he exits on angles, he can make Williams chase.

Soldic's debut risk is tempo shock. He has the tools to win exchanges, but Williams' bursts force immediate defensive responsibility; any slow read in the first round can become a momentum swing before Soldic settles into his preferred rhythm.

The fight may be decided by who touches the body first. Body work can blunt both men's explosive counters, and the fighter who invests downstairs early can make the later pocket exchanges less coin-flip dependent.

Gautier's finishing upside is real, but Kopylov is not the opponent to chase recklessly. Gautier should pressure behind feints and fence position, because straight-line blitzes give Kopylov the clean counter lanes he needs to slow the favorite's momentum.

Kopylov's best path is making Gautier work at kicking range before the pocket exchanges begin. If he lands to the body and exits before the return fire, he can turn a power matchup into a technical striking contest.

The grappling layer is the swing variable. Gautier can make Kopylov defend more than strikes if he mixes clinch pressure, but failed tie-ups would leave him in the exact mid-range where Kopylov's counters become cleaner.

Rodriguez's unbeaten record becomes more meaningful if he handles Coria's second and third looks. The premium question is not whether Rodriguez can start fast, but whether he can keep making correct reads after Coria changes rhythm.

Coria should test the prospect with phase changes rather than a single-note pace fight. Clinch interruptions, stance switches, and late-round flurries can make Rodriguez prove that his clean record is backed by composure under layered pressure.

Pinas' projection improves if he controls the center without loading up. He has enough finishing appeal that Pulyaev will be waiting for big entries, so Pinas needs patient pressure that turns Pulyaev before the power shots come.

Pulyaev's upset case is built around making the cleaner-record fighter uncomfortable early. If he can force Pinas to defend takedown looks, clinch returns, or awkward pocket exits, the matchup becomes less about record quality and more about adjustment speed.

McGhee's power and finishing history are most useful when he controls the first exchange after a reset. Sopaj can survive the headline weapons if he denies clean restarts and makes McGhee strike while turning or defending grips.

Sopaj's tactical route is to stretch the fight into layered minutes. If he can make McGhee defend kicks, clinch touches, and changing entries, he can test whether McGhee's ranked position is backed by defensive consistency.

The live signal is McGhee's reaction after Sopaj's first clean counter or level change. If McGhee stays patient, his power remains bankable; if he chases the response, Sopaj can make the fight swingier than the ranking suggests.

Unbeaten heavyweight fights often punish overconfidence, and this one is no different. Wint's extra pro experience helps only if he uses it to manage risk; trading clean in the first two minutes gives Armand the same chaos lane.

Armand's best read is whether Wint's quick turnaround leaves defensive gaps. If Wint starts fast but exits high, Armand can make him pay on counters; if Wint keeps the fight structured, Armand may have to prove his cardio and clinch defense.

Walker is most dangerous before the fight has a stable rhythm, so Parkin's first job is denying the wild opening. Low-risk jabs, clinch frames, and exits away from the power side can turn Walker's athletic chaos into isolated bursts.

Parkin's steadiness can win minutes, but he cannot let steadiness become passivity. Walker's highlight threat changes how judges and opponents react, so Parkin needs visible offense after defensive wins to make control feel like scoring.

The premium tell is Walker's balance after missed offense. If he resets cleanly, his length and power stay live; if he falls across his stance, Parkin can clinch, mat return, or counter in the moments where Walker is historically most vulnerable.

bouts.title: Rafael Dos Anjos vs Alexander Hernandez

items.fight_news: Dos Anjos' veteran path is pressure with purpose: force Hernandez backward, win underhooks, and make the younger athlete defend in layers. If he marches in without cutting angles, Hernandez still has the explosiveness to make entries costly.

Hernandez needs to avoid fighting in short emotional bursts. His athletic edge matters if he can touch, exit, and re-enter on his terms; it fades if Dos Anjos turns the bout into a grinding fence-and-clinch rhythm.
The rematch-style variable is patience. Dos Anjos can win by making the fight feel old and physical, while Hernandez needs fresh looks across all three rounds rather than one early speed advantage.

Vettori's pressure only works if he can make Naurdiev exchange after defending. Walking forward is not enough; he needs fence position, clinch touches, and return combinations that keep Naurdiev from simply circling into clean kicks.

Naurdiev's premium route is variety without wasted motion. If he layers kicks, body shots, and quick pivots, he can make Vettori chase; if he throws single shots and backs straight up, Vettori's durability and pressure become the safer read.

Scorecards may hinge on who owns the last 90 seconds of each round. Vettori often makes rounds feel hard late, while Naurdiev needs early technical success to remain visible once the exchanges get more physical.

McGee's veteran game is built to make opponents solve repeated pace questions. Nolan has to hurt him, clinch him, or clearly separate with counters; otherwise McGee can turn the opener into familiar volume and pressure rounds.

Nolan's finishing upside matters most in transition. Clean pocket exchanges are harder to sustain against McGee's experience, so Nolan should look for damage when McGee exits clinches, resets after shots, or squares up after combinations.

The late-round read is cardio under resistance. If Nolan's output drops after McGee forces contact, the veteran's minute-winning profile becomes stronger; if Nolan keeps his power after defending pressure, the underdog case stays alive.
